subtitle: Scholarly terms related to electoral processes and the mass media

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: the set of processes through which political actors, state institutions, the mass media and the public exchange politically relevant information and shape political meanings.

sections.label: Origin and scholarly development
sections.text: political communication is not a term coined by one person on a particular date. It is a field of study that developed where political science, sociology and communication research meet. Brian McNair's An Introduction to Political Communication, published by Routledge in 1995, is one of the works that set out the relationship between politics, media and democracy systematically. That date is not when the term first appeared; it is bibliographic evidence of the field being covered systematically in the scholarly literature.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: provides the theoretical basis for studying the activities of candidates and parties, campaign platforms, how voters are informed and how public opinion forms.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: the theory that by giving more attention to some issues, the mass media influence which problems the public sees as important.

sections.label: Key dates and authors
sections.text: American researchers Maxwell E. McCombs and Donald L. Shaw published The Agenda-Setting Function of Mass Media in 1972 in Public Opinion Quarterly (vol. 36, no. 2, pp. 176–187). The article examined the relationship between the issues the media covered during an election campaign and the issues voters considered important.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: used to analyse how much attention the media give to a particular candidate, problem or political issue.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: the process of highlighting certain aspects of an event or problem and presenting it within a particular frame of meaning.

sections.label: Key source
sections.text: American sociologist Erving Goffman's Frame Analysis: An Essay on the Organization of Experience was published in 1974. It examines social experience and how people make sense of situations through the concept of frames. The year of publication and authorship are also recorded in the WorldCat and Smithsonian Libraries and Archives catalogues.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: helps compare the headlines, context, commentary and evaluations through which the same political event is presented in different outlets.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: a media-effects mechanism: when the media emphasise certain issues, audiences rely more on the related criteria when judging political leaders and their performance.

sections.label: Key research dates and authors
sections.text: Shanto Iyengar, Mark D. Peters and Donald R. Kinder published Experimental Demonstrations of the “Not-So-Minimal” Consequences of Television News Programs in 1982 in the American Political Science Review. Through experiments, the authors showed that the problems television news covered more heavily affected how important viewers found those problems and how they judged the president's performance.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: useful for studying how a constant emphasis on certain topics in campaign coverage relates to the criteria voters use to judge candidates.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: an approach explaining that part of the information spread by the mass media first reaches opinion leaders and then passes from them to other people.

sections.label: Scholarly sources
sections.text: Paul F. Lazarsfeld, Bernard Berelson and Hazel Gaudet's The People's Choice was published in 1944. It studied the political decisions of voters in Erie County, Ohio, USA, and showed that personal conversations and the influence of acquaintances played an important part in voters' decisions. The two-step flow theory was later associated with the work of Lazarsfeld and his colleagues.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: helps study how campaign information spreads through journalists, political commentators, civic activists and other influential people.

terms.en: Аудитория эҳтиёжлари ва медиадан фойдаланиш ёндашуви

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: an approach that treats the audience not as passive recipients of information but as active participants who choose media and content to suit their own needs and goals.

sections.label: Key source
sections.text: Elihu Katz, Jay G. Blumler and Michael Gurevitch published Uses and Gratifications Research in 1973 in Public Opinion Quarterly (vol. 37, no. 4, pp. 509–523). The authors set out how to study systematically why people use media and what audiences need from them.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: useful for researching which platforms voters use, for what purposes, and to meet which information needs.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: the process by which activities, institutions and relationships in politics and other areas of society change under the influence of the media and the rules of media work.

sections.label: Scholarly development
sections.text: research on mediatization did not emerge in one step or from one author. The literature distinguishes several strands in how the concept took shape. For example, David L. Altheide and Robert P. Snow published Media Logic in 1979, and Kent Asp studied the mediatization of politics in 1986. Later, scholars such as Stig Hjarvard and Winfried Schulz developed the theoretical foundations of the concept.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: helps analyse how political parties, candidates and election bodies adapt their activity to media demands, news formats and distribution platforms.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: the overall expression of the views, attitudes and judgements of members of society on social and political issues. Public opinion need not be uniform or fixed; it can differ under the influence of different groups, information sources and social conditions.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: important for studying voters' attitudes to candidates, political platforms and the electoral process, and for analysing the relationship between media content and public opinion.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: the principle that different political views, interests, parties and social groups exist in a society and take part in political life.

sections.label: Origin
sections.text: political pluralism is not a single theory created by one author on a particular date. It took shape in political philosophy and political science over a long period. Rather than linking the concept to one book or year, it is more accurate to trace its development in political theory through independent literature.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: important when assessing how much space the media give to different parties, candidates and views.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: the social space in which citizens discuss matters of public importance, exchange views and form public opinion.

sections.label: Key date
sections.text: German philosopher Jürgen Habermas's Strukturwandel der Öffentlichkeit (The Structural Transformation of the Public Sphere) was published in 1962. It analyses the historical formation of the public sphere and its place in society. Although the concept was used in various senses before Habermas, his book holds an important place in its modern scholarly interpretation.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: helps explain the role of the media in enabling election debates, political discussion and citizen participation.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: newspapers, magazines, radio, television and other means of mass communication designed to deliver information to a wide audience.

sections.label: Origin
sections.text: the concept developed alongside the print press, mass publishing, radio and television. Establishing exactly when the term “mass media” was first used would require a dedicated etymological or historical source, so no single author or year is given.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: identifies the main institutions and channels that spread election information.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: mass media owned or controlled by the state.

sections.label: Origin
sections.text: the term describes a form of ownership and control. Naming a single originator or an exact year of origin would require reliable historical evidence.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: used to study how state-owned media report on elections, how editorially independent they are, and how they treat different political actors.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: media organisations whose ownership or control does not belong to the state. They may be private, public-service or non-profit; their legal status depends on national legislation.

sections.label: Origin
sections.text: the distinction between state and non-state media is not a theory devised by one person but a classification describing media ownership and institutional structure.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: makes it possible to compare how outlets with different forms of ownership cover an election campaign.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: a media organisation's professional principles and internal rules for selecting, verifying, preparing and publishing information, working with sources and ensuring impartiality.

sections.label: Origin
sections.text: editorial policy is a practical concept that took shape as the press and journalistic institutions developed. It is not accurate to attribute it to one person or a specific year.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: used to analyse the rules for giving candidates airtime and space, verifying information and managing conflicts of interest.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: the overall environment of media institutions, platforms, communication channels and audiences in which information is created, distributed and received.

sections.label: Origin
sections.text: the concept of media space broadened with the development of mass communication and digital technology. Without a reliable source, no conclusion can be drawn about when it was first used or who coined it.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: helps examine election information on television, in print, on websites and on social media as a single system.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: the sum of information sources, communication channels, technologies and information flows that people and organisations use.

sections.label: Origin
sections.text: the term is used differently in information science, communication studies, cybernetics and other fields. No single author or date of origin applies across all of them.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: makes it possible to study how voters use official information, journalistic content, political advertising and social media posts.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: the presence of diversity in information sources, ownership, opinions and views.

sections.label: Origin
sections.text: media pluralism developed through scholarly and legal debate about democratic society, press freedom and the media market. There is no basis for attributing it to any one person.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: used to assess whether voters have access to information about different political positions and platforms.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: competition between media organisations for audience attention, distribution channels, advertising revenue and position in the information market.

sections.label: Origin
sections.text: the concept developed in mass communication and media economics research. No single originator or date of first use is clearly established.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: helps analyse the speed of election reporting, headlines, presentation style and the contest for audiences.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: journalism based on gathering, verifying, preparing and distributing information and engaging with audiences using digital technology and the internet.

sections.label: Key period
sections.text: in Ramón Salaverría's article reviewing 25 years of research on digital journalism, 1994 is identified as the year the first web-based media appeared in several countries. This is an important point in the history of digital journalism, but it does not mean the term was coined that year.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: covers the rapid distribution of election information through websites, mobile devices and digital platforms.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: media formats and platforms that make it possible to create, store, process and distribute information in digital form.

sections.label: Origin
sections.text: the concept of digital media grew with the development of computer technology, digital communications and the internet. Its emergence cannot be tied to one author or date.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: describes how text, photos, video, audio, infographics and interactive data about elections are presented through digital channels.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: professional activity aimed at building relationships between an organisation or person and its publics, exchanging information and managing trust.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: helps explain how political organisations relate to the public and to journalists.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: communication activity aimed at planning and managing the relationships of political parties, candidates, state institutions or political movements with the public.

sections.label: Origin
sections.text: political PR took shape alongside modern public relations practice and the development of election campaigns. It is not justified to link it to one author and a single date. Research on the history of PR shows that the field became a profession in the 20th century.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: used to analyse how candidates work with the media, press conferences, statements, interviews and campaign information strategies.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: a plan drawn up in advance that sets out the audience, key messages, channels, resources and methods of evaluating results needed to achieve an organisation's communication goals.

sections.label: Origin
sections.text: PR strategy is not a single theory created by one person; it developed where strategic management and public relations practice meet.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: helps assess the consistency of a political actor's messages, audience engagement and media activity during an election period.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: a systematic approach that determines who should receive which message, through which channel and at what time, in order to achieve a set goal.

sections.label: Origin
sections.text: communication strategy is a broad concept used in many fields; its single originator or first year of use cannot be stated in general terms.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: serves to compare how parties, candidates and election bodies distribute information.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: the set of perceptions, judgements and associations about a political figure or organisation that has formed in the public mind.

sections.label: Origin
sections.text: political image is not a term that appeared on a particular date; it developed in research on political communication, social psychology, advertising and PR.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: important when analysing how the media portray a candidate's personal qualities, political experience, reputation and platform.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: the theory that the media's choice of which topics to cover more heavily influences which issues the public considers important.

sections.label: Key scholarly source
sections.text: the 1972 article by Maxwell McCombs and Donald Shaw. Using the 1968 US presidential election, the authors studied the relationship between the media agenda and the issues voters considered important.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: makes it possible to assess which topics the media cover more, which problems they neglect, and what place this choice has in the political information environment.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: the process of presenting an event or problem from a particular point of view and highlighting certain of its aspects.

sections.label: Key scholarly sources
sections.text: Erving Goffman's Frame Analysis was published in 1974. Later, in Framing: Toward Clarification of a Fractured Paradigm (1993), Robert M. Entman analysed the approaches in framing research and clarified the concept's place in communication studies.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: used to compare the content, headlines and context through which the same candidate or event is interpreted by different outlets.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: the mechanism by which the media, by covering certain issues more, affect the criteria audiences rely on when judging political figures or decisions.

sections.label: Scholarly development
sections.text: the 1982 experimental study by Shanto Iyengar, Mark D. Peters and Donald R. Kinder examined the relationship between the importance of issues in television news and judgements of the president's performance.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: helps analyse how the media agenda can affect how candidates are judged on the economy, security, corruption and other issues.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: the process by which the activities, institutions and communication practices of politics and other social spheres change under the influence of their relationship with the media.

sections.label: Sources in its development
sections.text: David L. Altheide and Robert P. Snow's Media Logic was published in 1979. Mediatization later developed into a distinct theoretical strand used to analyse how politics and other institutions interact with the media. Media Logic is one of the important sources in debates about mediatization, but the two concepts are not the same.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: makes it possible to analyse how political actors adapt their activity to media formats and audience attention.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: the exchange of information by organisations and institutions about their activities, decisions, goals and relations with the public.

sections.label: Origin
sections.text: the concept is used within organisational communication and institutional theory. Its single originator or exact year of origin cannot be stated without reliable evidence.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: important for studying the official information exchange of election commissions, state bodies, parties and media organisations.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: the process by which media content flows across different platforms, media organisations cooperate, and audiences move from one platform to another.

sections.label: Key scholarly source
sections.text: Henry Jenkins's Convergence Culture: Where Old and New Media Collide was published by New York University Press in 2006. Jenkins links convergence not only to technologies merging into one device but also to content moving across platforms and to cultural change.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: helps analyse how election coverage is distributed in different formats on websites, social media, television and mobile platforms.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: the process by which social, economic and cultural activity becomes increasingly tied to the infrastructure, rules and algorithms of digital platforms.

sections.label: Origin
sections.text: platformization is a concept that developed in contemporary media research on digital platforms. Claiming that a particular person coined it or that it appeared in a particular year would require further historical verification.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: used to study the role of social media in distributing, recommending and delivering political information to audiences.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: the quality of presenting information in several forms, such as text, images, sound, video, animation and interactive elements.

sections.label: Origin
sections.text: the modern use of the term multimedia expanded with the development of computer and digital technology. Without a reliable dedicated source on when the term was first used, no exact year is given.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: describes how election news is delivered through text, infographics, video commentary, audio and interactive visualisations.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: the ability of users or audiences to interact with media content, the way it is presented, or the people who produce it.

sections.label: Origin
sections.text: the concept of interactivity is used in different senses in research on computer interfaces, communication theory and digital media. Rather than asserting flatly that it has no single originator or date, it is better to study its development separately in each field.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: helps analyse online polls, comments, Q&A sessions, live broadcasts and mechanisms for collecting audience views.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: a response returned by the person or audience receiving information to the sender or to the system.

sections.label: Origin
sections.text: the concept of feedback is used not only in communication but also in cybernetics and control theory. Norbert Wiener's Cybernetics: Or Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine, published in 1948, is one of the important sources in the scholarly development of feedback in control and communication. This does not mean that Wiener coined the term.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: used to assess how audience questions, objections, comments and requests are taken into account in media work.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: an information system in which traditional and digital media, political actors and audiences operate in interconnection.

sections.label: Key scholarly source
sections.text: Andrew Chadwick's The Hybrid Media System: Politics and Power was published in 2013. The author analysed the interdependence of the logics, institutions and actors of older and newer media in political communication.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: makes it possible to analyse comprehensively how television, newspapers, websites, social media and political actors influence one another.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: the use of computer algorithms to show, rank or recommend information to users.

sections.label: Origin
sections.text: algorithmic curation is linked to the development of digital platforms, search engines and recommendation systems. Identifying a single originator or date of first use would require a dedicated historical source.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: important for studying the order in which election news is shown to audiences and how platform algorithms can affect the visibility of information.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: the group of people who receive, follow or use a particular media product.

sections.label: Origin
sections.text: the concept of the audience developed with forms of communication from theatre and public speaking to the print press, radio, television and digital media. Its interpretation in modern media research has been shaped by several scholarly traditions.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: helps study who receives election information, what information they need and which media they choose.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: a concept describing audiences' attention to media content, their use of it, their reactions and their participation in conversation.

sections.label: Origin
sections.text: audience engagement has been defined and measured in different ways in media research. Online it can include comments, shares, reactions, reading time and other metrics. There is no single originator or date that applies in all cases.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: used to study how actively audiences engage with election content.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: the number or share of an audience that information or a media product reached over a given period.

sections.label: Origin
sections.text: measuring reach developed with audience measurement methods in radio, television, advertising and media research. The exact way it is measured depends on the platform and the research methodology.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: important for assessing how many people election news reached. Reach cannot be equated with the audience having read the material in full or having believed it.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: the system of theoretical foundations, concepts, principles and scientific methods used to explain a research problem.

sections.label: Origin
sections.text: the term belongs to general scientific methodology; it is not a specific media theory created by one person.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: determines which theories and methods are used to study media content, audience response and communication effectiveness in election coverage.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: research based on observation, experiment, questionnaires, interviews, documents or other data.

sections.label: Origin
sections.text: the idea of empirical knowledge goes back to philosophical traditions long before modern science took shape. It cannot be tied to one author or a single date.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: used to collect media content, survey voters and assess media performance on the basis of concrete data.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: a method of systematically analysing text, images, audio, video or other communication content according to set rules. It can be quantitative or qualitative.

sections.label: Key source
sections.text: Bernard Berelson's Content Analysis in Communication Research was published in 1952. It set out content analysis as a systematic method for communication research. Although Berelson's work was an important milestone, analysing the content of texts predates it.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: used to code and compare the number of stories about candidates, topics, headlines, sources and the way judgements are made.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: the process of tracking, collecting, sorting and analysing information on a given topic over a set period.

sections.label: Origin
sections.text: media monitoring grew out of press-clipping and press-review practice and later the monitoring of radio, television and digital information. Naming a single originator or exact year of origin would require a dedicated historical source.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: makes it possible to track regularly how candidates, parties and election topics are covered in the media during an election period.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: a set of analytical methods that study how meaning, social relations, views and power relations are formed through language and communication.

sections.label: Scholarly development
sections.text: discourse analysis took shape in various theoretical schools. For example, Teun A. van Dijk's News as Discourse was published in 1988 and is considered an important source for analysing news texts from a discourse perspective. That is not the year discourse analysis first appeared.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: used to study how candidates are described in political texts, which concepts recur, and how political events are interpreted.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: a method of comparing two or more objects, situations, sources or periods against set criteria.

sections.label: Origin
sections.text: comparison is one of the general methods of scientific inquiry, not a distinct media theory created by any one person.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: makes it possible to compare the information content of state and non-state media, different media platforms or different election campaigns.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: a method of watching and recording the characteristics and changes of a research object according to a predetermined procedure.

sections.label: Origin
sections.text: observation is one of the oldest methods of scientific research; it has no single originator or date of origin.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: used to record systematically media activity during elections, press conferences, journalistic events or conversations on digital platforms.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: a method of collecting people's views, experiences, behaviour or information through standardised questions.

sections.label: Key period
sections.text: mass polling and methods of measuring voter opinion developed widely in the 20th century. Gallup's historical materials identify the 1930s as an important period in the development of modern public opinion polling in the United States. This does not mean that Gallup invented the survey method.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: used to study voters' information sources, trust in the media and awareness of the election.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: drawing on different people, organisations, documents and points of view in news content.

sections.label: Origin
sections.text: the term is linked to the principles of working with sources in journalism, information quality and media pluralism. No single originator or date of origin is established.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: important for determining whether election news relies on a single political actor or official source, or covers a range of views.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: the effort to present the relevant important viewpoints and parties to a story fairly and in context.

sections.label: Origin
sections.text: balanced reporting is a normative principle linked to journalistic ethics and professional standards. No single originator or exact date of origin can be given.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: important when covering different candidates, setting out their positions and checking political claims. Balance does not automatically mean giving each side equal time; context and evidence must also be taken into account.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: the set of properties of information such as relevance, accuracy, completeness, timeliness, clarity and reliability.

sections.label: Origin
sections.text: assessing information quality developed through different criteria in research on information systems, records management, journalism and management. There is no single author or date for all fields.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: used to assess how correct, complete, current and useful election news is for the audience.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: the grounds for trusting information or its source, including the source's reputation, evidence, verifiability and the consistency of the data.

sections.label: Origin
sections.text: credibility has been studied in several research traditions in communication, psychology, journalism and information science. It has no single originator or year of origin.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: used to assess whether news about candidates and the electoral process relies on trustworthy sources, checks facts and avoids false information.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: the correspondence of the facts, names, dates, figures and other details in a story to reality.

sections.label: Origin
sections.text: accuracy is one of the basic requirements of fact-checking and professional journalistic standards. It is not a theory created by any particular scholar.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: important when checking that the election date, voting procedure, information about candidates and results are reported without errors.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: preparing information and delivering it to the audience at the right time relative to the event or process.

sections.label: Origin
sections.text: timeliness is a professional criterion in journalism linked to the currency of information and the news production process. It cannot be tied to one author or date.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: used to assess whether important changes in the electoral process, official decisions and results are reported without delay. Timeliness does not, however, remove the requirement to check facts.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: a concept expressing how far the result of communication has achieved its set goals. Effectiveness can be measured by whether a message reached the audience, was understood, was remembered or influenced the intended action.

sections.label: Origin
sections.text: the concept is used in different ways in communication theory, organisational management and evaluation research. Naming a single originator or exact year of origin would require a dedicated source.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: helps assess whether election content reached its target audience, was clear, and how well it met information needs.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: the acceptance by society of an institution's or authority's powers and activities as lawful, acceptable or justified.

sections.label: Key sources
sections.text: Max Weber's work on authority and legitimacy holds an important place in the development of this concept in sociology. Institutional legitimacy was later studied widely in organisation theory as well. When choosing a specific work and year of publication, Weber's various works and their publication history need to be distinguished.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: used to analyse media content on how the public accepts election institutions, electoral rules and results. Legitimacy cannot be measured through media coverage alone.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: a model for assessing media coverage of electoral processes against several criteria.

sections.label: Important clarification
sections.text: the MS–7 model was developed by the University of Journalism and Mass Communications of Uzbekistan and Jamshid Namozov. On 30 July 2026, the Intellectual Property Center under the Ministry of Justice of the Republic of Uzbekistan issued certificate of deposit No. 010589.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: the system is designed for the comprehensive assessment, monitoring and comparative analysis (ranking) of how digital mass media cover electoral processes, based on a single scientific and innovative approach.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: SMSI is a composite index expressing how effectively the media cover an election.

SMSI (Saylov Media Samaradorligi Indexi, the Election Media Effectiveness Index) was developed to express assessment results as a single numerical indicator. It makes it possible to measure numerically how effectively digital media cover electoral processes, compare platforms, build rankings and track development over time.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: a comprehensive methodology has been developed for assessing how effectively digital mass media cover electoral processes.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: a method of assessing an object or process not by a single indicator but by several interrelated criteria and dimensions.

sections.label: Origin
sections.text: comprehensive assessment is a general methodological approach used in many fields of research.

sections.label: Relevance to election journalism
sections.text: makes it possible to analyse media content not only by volume or reach but also by quality of content, source diversity, accuracy and other criteria.

sections.label: Definition
sections.text: an indicator that expresses the overall state of a complex phenomenon or object by combining several separate indicators in a set way.

sections.label: Scientific and methodological basis
sections.text: integral or composite indicators are used in many fields. One of the international methodological sources on them is the Handbook on Constructing Composite Indicators: Methodology and User Guide (2008), prepared by the OECD and the European Commission's Joint Research Centre. It describes stages such as selecting indicators, normalisation, weighting and aggregation.
